newsitem.title: USA: Reich says U.S. wages rising, inflation not a threat.
newsitem.headline: Reich says U.S. wages rising, inflation not a threat.

text.p: Wages of U.S. workers appear to be edging higher after a 15-year decline but the new trend poses no threat to inflation, Labour Secretary Robert Reich said Wednesday.

"Wages for most workers, which have been stagnant for years, are now turning up," Reich said in an interview with Reuters in which he highlighted key points of a speech to be delivered later to an economists' group in Boston.
"They are turning up at a healthy rate," he said.
As evidence of the pickup in wages, Reich pointed to the 3.6 percent increase in average hourly earnings in the twelve months ended in August 1996 -- an increase that exceeds the rate of inflation.

He also noted that since the first quarter of this year, the wage component of the Employment Cost Index has shown an upward trend, although recent slow growth in benefit costs has held down overall compensation costs.

With unemployment nationally at a seven-year low of 5.1 percent and even lower in some parts of the country, Reich said labour markets are "getting a little tighter," which is helping to set the stage for rising wages.

However, in a draft copy of his speech, which will be delivered at 1 p.m. EDT (1700 GMT) to the National Association of Business Economists, Reich took aim at theories suggesting that the low unemployment will lead to higher inflation.
"Structural changes in the American economy suggest why we can sustain a lower level of unemployment than we had previously assumed, without risking inflation," Reich said.
He said he believed that over the long term, the unemployment rate could fall further without igniting inflation, though he said it was unclear how much further.
A number of economists and some Federal Reserve officials have expressed concern that the jobless rate is currently at a level that may pose an inflationary threat.
Reich stressed that, in keeping with the policy of the Clinton administration, he was not commenting on policies of the Fed.
Still, he suggested that in weighing greater employment against avoidance of inflation, the needs of those who might become "casualties" in the war against inflation should be taken into account.

Citing a new study by Brookings Institution economists that argues that zero inflation could be accompanied by a permanent loss in employment, Reich said, "At the least, we should demand a burden of proof from those who argue that zero inflation is an appropriate goal."
Inflation, as measured by the Labour Deparment's Consumer Price Index, rose 3.0 percent in the year ended in July. Figures for August are due out Friday.
Regarding the overall economy, Reich said a "vigorous expansion" was under way, but added that there is "no sign of accelerating inflation."
On Tuesday, Fed Governor Janet Yellen cautioned that there is "definitely a chance inflation will rise," although she added: "The evidence isn't utterly definitive we're going to see inflation rise."

The Fed's next policy-making meeting is scheduled for Sept. 24, and economists have mixed views as to whether the central bank will raise short-term interest rates to head off inflation. Such a move, if it occurred, would be the first rate increase in about 1-1/2 years and could jeopardise the 5-1/2-year-old economic expansion.
Reich said there seemed to be some signs that the economy was beginning to slow, but that it was unclear by how much.
